evangelical.salvation:
Evangelicals speak of being saved as a personal turning to Jesus Christ: you repent of sin, trust his finished work on the cross, and receive forgiveness and new life as a gift. Salvation is by grace through faith, not by earning God's favor through church membership, sacraments, or moral effort, though a changed life is expected to follow.

Many evangelicals describe a definite moment when they were saved; others speak of a longer process of coming to faith. Almost all insist that you can know you belong to Christ in this life, and that the gospel must be offered to every person.
evangelical.new_birth:
To be born again is, for evangelicals, the inward work of the Holy Spirit that makes a person a new creation in Christ. Jesus' words to Nicodemus are taken as a requirement for every believer, not a metaphor reserved for baptism or church initiation. The new birth is God's act; it is received by repentance and faith.

Evangelicals differ on whether this always happens in a dated conversion experience or sometimes quietly in a Christian home, but they agree that without the new birth a person is not yet a Christian in the living sense, however religious the upbringing.
evangelical.baptism_in_the_spirit:
Evangelicals commonly speak of the filling of the Spirit as the Spirit's ongoing work of empowering, convicting, and making Christ known. Most hold that every true believer already has the Holy Spirit from conversion. Filling is then asked for again and again as the believer yields to God.

Charismatic evangelicals may also speak of a later baptism in the Spirit with gifts such as tongues. Non-charismatic evangelicals usually treat that language as confusing or unhelpful and keep the older wording of filling, walking in the Spirit, and being led by the Spirit.
evangelical.continuationism:
Evangelicals do not agree about the sign gifts. Continuationists believe gifts such as prophecy, tongues, and healing still operate under Scripture's authority. Cessationists believe those sign gifts belonged to the apostolic age and are not the church's ordinary equipment now.

Both sides usually accept that God still heals and guides. The charismatic question is whether such works come through standing offices and gifts like those in 1 Corinthians 12, or through providence and answered prayer without restoring the New Testament sign gifts as a norm.
evangelical.perseverance:
Many evangelicals, especially in Baptist and Reformed-leaning circles, teach eternal security: those who are truly saved will be kept by God and will not be lost. The popular phrase once saved always saved names that confidence, though careful teachers add that a life with no fruit raises the question whether the person was ever converted.

Wesleyan and Holiness evangelicals reject that formula. They teach that a believer can fall from grace by persistent unbelief or willful sin. Across the movement, perseverance is spoken of as God's keeping and as the believer's call to endure.
evangelical.assurance:
Assurance is the God-given confidence that you are saved. Evangelicals look for it in the promises of Scripture, the finished work of Christ, and the Spirit's witness with the believer's spirit, often joined to evidence of a changed life.

This knowing you are saved is treated as normal Christian experience, not presumption. Doubts are common and are met by looking again to Christ rather than by treating uncertainty as a virtue. Traditions that warn against claiming certainty in this life sound foreign to most evangelical preaching.
evangelical.inerrancy:
Inerrancy, for the mainstream of modern evangelicalism, means that Scripture, in the autographs, is without error in all that it affirms, because it is God's Word. Infallibility of Scripture is used in a closely related sense: the Bible will not fail as a rule of faith and life.

Not every evangelical uses the word inerrancy. Some prefer infallible or trustworthy and allow more room for genre, rounding, or ancient description of the world. Even they typically refuse the idea that the Bible teaches theological or moral falsehood.
evangelical.ecumenism:
Evangelicals are often wary of official church-union schemes that they think blur the gospel. Cooperation is the more natural word: shared evangelism, relief work, and fellowship among those who confess the same Christ and the same Scriptures.

Bodies such as the World Evangelical Alliance express that instinct. Some evangelicals join wider ecumenical councils; many do not. The test is usually whether Jesus Christ as unique Saviour and the authority of the Bible remain central, not whether a single visible church is reconstructed.
evangelical.sacred_music:
Evangelical worship music ranges from inherited hymns to contemporary worship songs led by a band. The argument is rarely whether music itself belongs in gathered worship; it is which style helps a congregation sing the gospel with understanding and affection.

Hymns remain a standard in many churches. Contemporary worship became widespread from the late twentieth century. Critics inside the movement worry about entertainment or thin doctrine; defenders say new songs can carry the same truths. Practice varies congregation by congregation.
evangelical.altar_call:
The altar call, or invitation, is a public appeal at the end of a sermon for hearers to come forward, pray, or otherwise mark that they are trusting Christ or renewing obedience. It grew with revival preaching and remains common in many Baptist, Holiness, and Pentecostal-leaning evangelical churches.

Other evangelicals, especially Reformed ones, reject a standing invitation as a man-made addition that can manufacture false conversions. They still call for repentance and faith, but they locate the response in the heart and in later baptism or church care rather than in walking an aisle.
evangelical.millennium:
Evangelicals read Revelation 20 in more than one way. Premillennialism expects Christ to return before a thousand-year reign. Amillennialism treats the thousand years as the present reign of Christ. Postmillennialism expects a long era of gospel success before the return.

Dispensational premillennialism has been especially influential in American evangelicalism. None of these schemes is required by the word evangelical itself; the shared conviction is that Christ will return in glory and that history is in his hands.
evangelical.rapture:
The rapture names the hope that living believers will be caught up to meet the Lord when he comes, drawn from 1 Thessalonians 4. In popular evangelical use it often means a coming of Christ for the church that is distinct from his public appearing to judge the world.

That two-stage reading is common among dispensational evangelicals and is disputed by others who see one return of Christ. All sides that use the word agree that the Lord's coming is personal and visible and that the dead in Christ will rise.
evangelical.abortion:
Mainstream evangelical teaching holds that the unborn child is a human life made in God's image and that abortion is therefore a grave moral wrong except, in some statements, where the mother's life is in immediate danger. The movement became publicly identified with this stance in the late twentieth century.

Pastoral practice usually pairs the prohibition with an offer of forgiveness in Christ for those who have had an abortion and with support for pregnancy care. A minority of self-identified evangelicals argue for a more permissive civil law; that view is not the received teaching of the large evangelical bodies.
evangelical.sexual_ethics:
Evangelicals typically speak of biblical sexual ethics: sexual union belongs in the covenant of marriage between a man and a woman, and extra-marital sex, including homosexual practice, is sin. Desire itself is not treated as identity in the same way some wider cultures now treat it; the call is repentance and costly obedience with pastoral care.

A smaller evangelical left reads the same texts differently and blesses same-sex marriages. That reading is rejected by the major evangelical fellowships and confessional statements, which treat the historic reading as a matter of obedience to Scripture rather than of mere custom.
evangelical.tithing:
Many evangelical churches teach the tithe, a tenth of income given to the Lord's work, as a biblical starting point for generosity, often directed first to the local congregation. Others refuse to bind the Mosaic tenth on Gentile believers and speak instead of cheerful, sacrificial giving.

Tithing sermons are common; so is the warning that giving cannot buy salvation. Prosperity teaching that treats the tithe as a guaranteed investment is widespread on the movement's fringe and is criticised by other evangelicals as a distortion of grace.
evangelical.headship:
Evangelicals divide over how men and women share authority in home and church. Complementarianism teaches headship: men and women are equal in worth but are given different offices, usually including a male-only eldership and a husband's responsibility to lead the family. Egalitarianism teaches that the Spirit gifts women and men alike for every office.

Both camps claim Scripture. The split is one of the most visible inner arguments in evangelicalism, and congregations and seminaries often identify themselves by which side they take.
evangelical.separated_brethren:
Evangelicals readily call other evangelicals other believers when the gospel of Christ crucified and risen, received by faith, is confessed. They are slower with Christians whose churches they think have added works, a different gospel, or a Christ who is not fully God and man.

Nominal Christians names the concern that baptism, family religion, or church rolls can exist without conversion. The line is drawn less by denomination than by whether a person has trusted Christ. That habit can sound ungenerous to traditions that locate belonging in the sacrament and the visible church.
